Tanzania;
Tanzanian Beaches Are Treasure Troves
Africa News
May 2, 2003 Friday


Copyright 2003 AllAfrica, Inc.
Length: 777 words
Byline: Business Times
Body


TANZANIA is blessed with beautiful beaches, but most of them are hardly developed for tourism purposes, a study has shown.
If those beaches were developed, tourists would be attracted and more jobs could be created.
Now the Ministry of Natural Resources and Tourism is interested in developing them by opening doors to private investors.
The North-South Coast's palm-fringed beaches straddle from Pangani in the upper northern part via the beaches of Bagamoyo, the islands off shore and south of Dar esc Salaam to Mafia island, Kilwa, Lindi and finally to Msimbati, near the border of Mozambique.
Only this makes Tanzania unique in tourism development and able to produce more jobs to hundreds of youngsters.
According to the Integrated Tourism Master Plan Update of Tanzania, Pangani possesses an arguably the best beaches on the stretch between Bagamoyo and Tanga.
The ministry hopes that a recent establishment of several small-scale, inexpensive resorts south of Pangani will help develop the beaches.
The development of the North East Mountain Zone will, in the long run, function as the beach complement to a combined safari and nature holidaymakers, according to the ministry's master plan.
This is an important feature of the zone between Bagamoyo in the north and Buyuni in the south of Dar esc Salaam.
As the commercial centre of the country, all the main roads of the country eventually lead to Dar es Salaam and through the harbour access is provided from the sea. There is also the Dar es Salaam International Airport.
According to a Development Framework Circuit Study, the city has been earmarked as an important centre for tourism, not just a transfer hub alone.
"Proposals are made to develop and improve the waterfront as well as improve the South East Coast by developing small-scale, luxury holiday resorts," the framework indicates.
"In the view of its location and the absence of other attractions in the immediate vicinity, the focus would be primarily beach oriented. This would place a higher emphasis on the proposed operation being self-contained."
The same study views Bagamoyo as an upcoming tourism area. Besides having good beaches and being close to Saadani National Park, it is only a short trip by boat from Bagamoyo to a historic island of Zanzibar.
"There is an opportunity here to turn the travel element into part of the product experience. Movement from one location to another along the coast would be more enjoyable and more comfortable if it were undertaken by boat rather than land," the study says. "The opportunity to run excursions from Bagamoyo to Saadani with its unique coastal frontage is one."
Other obvious boat excursions, according to study, are between Bagamoyo and Zanzibar and Bagamoyo and Dar es Salaam. Likewise, the beach resort area, north of Bagamoyo could be linked to Dar es Salaam by boat.
Moreover, Mafia Island represents an attractive proportion for the development of special interest tourism.
"The Marine Park area in particular is known to have excellent diving and snorkeling with 12 dive sites already identified," it explains.
Alongside, deep-sea fishing in the waters surrounding Mafia is considered to be of world-class status, though hardly tapped.
Attractive beaches are found on the northwest and south coast. The true potential of the Island lies in exploiting the islands off the beaten track character and developing small-scale, inexpensive but stylish accommodation. Thereby presenting a model of low impact-high value tourism.
Possibly, Mafia could become a strong option on the Southern Circuit and should be developed with a view to catering to those who want a very relaxed, quiet holiday and are content with this part of their holiday depending on the beach, activities related to the marine environment and good facilities and service.
"An interesting possibility is to link Mafia Island to the Rufiji Delta, to provide a memorable journey along the Rufiji River into the Selous," the study observes.
More fortune to the tourism sector, some of towns along the beaches have been declared the world heritage site. Among those are Bagamoyo and Kilwa.
Kilwa, which has for a long time regarded as the most important town on the Swahili coast as the ruins of the building suggest, is geared towards special interest tourism, history and archaeology.
The old town has some fine beaches, which could be used as a starting point for establishing some medium-scale resorts of high quality, to cater for an important upmarket clientele that combines a Selous/Ruaha safari with an add on beach product of similar quality.
